subject: ela
description: Students write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence. They introduce a clear claim, organize the reasons and evidence logically, support the claim with reasons backed by credible evidence drawn from a provided source, use words and phrases to clarify the relationships among claim and reasons, establish and maintain a formal style, and provide a concluding statement that follows from the argument. Because this is a writing standard, every item embeds the full prompt, sentence, paragraph, or short source text it depends on inside the item itself, so the student needs nothing external. Items test the components of argument writing through analysis, selection, and short construction rather than full multi-paragraph essays.
subSkills: Introduce a clear claim (a debatable position, not a fact or topic) that responds to the writing prompt
Distinguish a claim from a counterclaim, a reason, and a piece of evidence
Support a claim with logical reasons and pair each reason with relevant, credible evidence from a provided source
Distinguish relevant evidence that supports the claim from irrelevant or off-topic detail
Organize reasons and evidence in a logical order so the argument builds clearly
Use transitional words and phrases (for example, because, therefore, in addition, for instance, however) to clarify the relationship between the claim and the reasons and evidence
Establish and maintain a formal style, avoiding slang, contractions, first-person opinion fillers, and emotional or biased language
Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from and reinforces the argument presented

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the claim
problemArchetypes.example: Read the prompt and the four sentences. 'Prompt: Should students be allowed to use phones during lunch?' Sentence A: 'Phones can connect to the school wifi.' Sentence B: 'Students should be allowed to use phones during lunch because lunch is free time.' Sentence C: 'Many students own phones.' Sentence D: 'Lunch lasts thirty minutes.' Which sentence states a clear, debatable claim? Answer: B, because it takes a position that someone could argue against and answers the prompt.

problemArchetypes.name: Match relevant evidence to a reason
problemArchetypes.example: Claim: 'Our school should plant a garden.' Reason: 'A garden would give students fresh vegetables.' Read the source line: 'A 2021 school survey found that 68 percent of students rarely eat fresh vegetables at home.' Which choice is the most relevant evidence for this reason? Answer: the survey statistic, because it directly supports the need for fresh vegetables, while a fact about garden colors or soil cost does not.

problemArchetypes.name: Spot the irrelevant evidence
problemArchetypes.example: Claim: 'Recess should be longer.' Read the short passage in the item. Three sentences support the claim with evidence about focus and exercise; one sentence says 'The cafeteria serves pizza on Fridays.' Which sentence is irrelevant to the argument and should be removed? Answer: the pizza sentence, because it does not support the claim that recess should be longer.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the best transition
problemArchetypes.example: Read the two sentences embedded in the item: 'Reading every day builds vocabulary. ____, students who read often score higher on tests.' Which transition best clarifies the relationship? Options: 'However,' 'In contrast,' 'In addition,' 'Although.' Answer: 'In addition,' because the second sentence adds supporting evidence rather than contrasting.

problemArchetypes.name: Maintain formal style
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence from a student argument: 'Honestly, homework is super annoying and nobody likes it, so we should ditch it.' Which revision keeps a formal style appropriate for an argument? Answer: 'Homework places an unnecessary burden on students and should be reduced.'

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the concluding statement
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short argument paragraph embedded in the item that argues for a later school start time using two reasons. Which concluding statement best follows from the argument? Answer: the sentence that restates the claim and reflects the reasons given, not a new unrelated idea or a single repeated detail.

Easy.description: A single sentence or a pair of short sentences (roughly 10 to 25 words total) embedded in the item, with a clearly stated prompt or claim. The task is identify-level: pick the claim, name whether a sentence is a claim or a fact, choose an obvious relevant piece of evidence, or select a single clear transition. Only one component of argument writing is tested and the correct answer is unmistakable.
constraints: Stimulus is one short sentence or a two-sentence pair included in the prompt
Tests exactly one component (claim vs fact, single transition, one obvious relevant detail)
Identify-level task: select or label, no construction required
Distractors are clearly weaker (a fact, a topic, or an obviously off-topic detail)

Medium.description: A short paragraph or a claim plus a 3 to 5 line provided source (roughly 30 to 60 words) embedded in the item. The task is analyze-level: match the most relevant evidence to a specific reason, identify which of several sentences is irrelevant and should be cut, choose the transition that best fits a logical relationship among several plausible options, or fix an informal sentence to maintain a formal style. The student must weigh more than one option that is partly defensible.
constraints: Stimulus is a short paragraph or a claim with a brief source passage in the prompt
Tests evidence relevance, logical organization, transition choice, or formal style
Analyze-level task: choose or revise based on how well a part supports the claim
Distractors are plausible partial fits (related but less relevant evidence, a transition of the wrong relationship)

Hard.description: A multi-sentence argument paragraph or two short related sources (roughly 60 to 110 words) embedded in the item, sometimes containing a flaw to repair. The task is evaluate-level: judge which concluding statement best follows from the full argument, choose the strongest reason-and-evidence pairing among several, decide which revision most improves the logical flow or formality across the paragraph, or determine why a piece of evidence fails to support the claim and what would strengthen it. Requires inference about the writer's intent and how the parts of the argument fit together.
constraints: Stimulus is a 3 to 6 sentence argument paragraph or two short sources included in the prompt
Tests how multiple components interact: claim, reasons, evidence, organization, conclusion
Evaluate-level task: select the best full revision or conclusion and justify it against the argument
Requires inference to judge logical fit, relevance, and whether the conclusion follows from the reasons

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses a topic or a fact with a claim, choosing a statement that no one could argue against
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'Many students own phones' or 'The topic is school lunch' as the claim instead of a debatable position such as 'Students should be allowed phones at lunch'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats any evidence about the general topic as relevant, ignoring whether it actually supports the specific reason or claim
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a true but off-point detail (the cafeteria serves pizza on Fridays) as support for 'recess should be longer' because it mentions school

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses a reason with evidence, offering an opinion restatement where a fact, statistic, or example is needed
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses 'because it is a good idea' or 'because everyone thinks so' as the evidence instead of a concrete fact from the source

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student selects a transition that signals the wrong logical relationship, such as a contrast word where an addition or cause word is needed
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Inserts 'However' or 'In contrast' between two sentences that actually add supporting evidence, instead of 'In addition' or 'Therefore'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student accepts informal or emotional language as appropriate for an argument, keeping slang, contractions, or first-person filler
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Keeps 'Honestly, homework is super annoying and nobody likes it' instead of a formal revision

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a conclusion that introduces a brand-new idea or simply repeats one minor detail rather than restating the claim and reflecting the reasons
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an ending that adds an unrelated point or echoes a single example, instead of a statement that follows from the whole argument

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses the most strongly worded or emotional sentence as the best argument, mistaking forceful language for logical support
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects an exaggerated claim such as 'This rule is the worst thing ever' as the strongest argument instead of the reasoned, evidence-backed sentence
